items.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from ba
items.content:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

items.content:
New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

items.content:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

items.content:
HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says ChatGPT and Claude are the new browsers, and like browsers, they won't own the whole software stack:

"Everything kind of comes back around again. When we saw the original SaaS development moving to the web-based application world, we had the same kind of thing. We had client-server apps running on our desktops. And then we had this browser thing come along, Internet Explorer and later Mozilla."

"But as it turns out, Google did not own the entire application stack. There were lots and lots of software companies that got built. The interface became the browser because that was a convenient way to get to the actual product that you needed to get to."

"We have a similar thing now. And it's different, because the AI is doing cognition work, it's doing actual smart things. But if you just look at the ChatGPT and Claude Cowork thing, they're effectively the new OS. They are the new browsers. And there will be companies like HubSpot that sort of plug in."

@dharmesh

items.content:
HubSpot co-founder and CTO Dharmesh Shah says it's less scary to build an AI startup now than in 2023, as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road the frontier labs are following:

"The frontier model companies have invested hundreds of billions of dollars building, doing the pre-training. And so their whole business effectively now is taking the capex that they've spent and the money they're continuing to spend and saying, 'How do we sell inference? How do we sell tokens? How do we monetize the thing that we've built?'"

"There are SaaS companies and startups that know their particular domain, know their market, have some distribution, or have something that allows them to sell tokens and be a reseller of inference."

"Think of AI as infrastructure in the same way we thought of AWS and cloud infrastructure 15 years ago... I think it's less scary now to build in and around the AI arena than it was in 2023."

"We have open source. We have lots of great commercial products. So as long as you stay off the Yellow Brick Road, it is completely possible now that you're not gonna get margined out, because you have options."

items.content:
Martin Casado on how AI breaks The Mythical Man-Month:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. The Mythical Man-Month is the Mythical Man-Month for a reason."

"Ten years ago, if I had five founders show up and they asked for a billion dollars and I gave it to them, what would happen?"

"They would detonate, right? They would hire a bunch of engineers, and then you're really fucked, right? You can't throw capital in it."

"To me, the biggest shift, industrial-revolution-level shift with AI, is I can take 20 people and I can give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Now, do they make $500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new and is so interesting."

@martin_casado with @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

"When you would go show up for a pitch at CAA in 1990 where I think they had like 90% market share, they would sit around a table, and Michael would introduce you as Robert Redford and say, 'Look, meet my colleague who does nothing other than radio deals. Here's my expert in radio deals. Here's my expert in international. Here's my expert in books.'"

"And we basically took the same model to the VC world. The VC world was a lot like that. You had a one-to-one relationship with John Doerr, who was fantastic at what he did."

"As the domains grew, the expertise needed just continued to grow."

"Let's hire GPs who are functional domain experts in the particular areas of investing they want, and then let's surround them with this phalanx of somebody who all they do all day long is manage CFO relationships, or CEO relationships, or VPs of engineering, somebody who all they do is government relations, or business development."

7/ agents are only open to us ecommerce and online services right now. plumbers, dentists etc are next, and so lots of opportunity to help main street here

9/ i’m not sure people want to talk to a brand’s agent. i think they’ll want their own agent to talk to it for them

10/ 1.2 billion people use chatgpt every week. i’d go claim my profile before finishing this post if you can

I really love using Fable 5.2. On big, open-ended work it feels like a major step above Opus 5.5. 

A few tips for getting the most out of it:
- Ask what’s wrong with your idea before it builds anything. It’s great at brainstorming and will push back
- Start on med/high effort, and save xhigh for hardest problems
- Tell it up front what needs your approval (e.g. deleting things) and that the rest is its call
- Give it a whole project instead of a next step and let it run for hours. This is where it shines

Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI r
items.content:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

> Use Fable 5.2 for all planning and brainstorming
> Go back and forth on your idea until it feels super ironed out
> Have it create incredibly detailed tasks in your favorite task manager (linear/notion/whatever)
> Switch to Opus 5.5

> Have Sonnet or even Haiku subagents test

Fable 5.2 is the most intelligent model ever created

If you have it make detailed enough tasks and have it plan the idea out thoroughly enough, you do NOT need it to do all the execution

This set up will get you better results and save you tons of tokens, trust me

You need to run the prompt below in Grok Bot/Duet/Dots

It's saved me more time than any other single prompt I've run

The biggest issue with agents is you use it to 1% of it's capability. You only automate 1% of the work it can actually take care of

This fixes that

Prompt:

My goal for working with you is to lighten my cognitive load. I want to get more work done, but with less effort on my part. Based on what you know about me and what we do together, what are some things we can do, systems we can implement, subagents we can build, or routines we can create to accomplish this goal?

This will cause your agent to review everything it knows about you and the work you've done together, and come up with systems that 'lighten your cognitive load'

For me this is the biggest benefit of AI

I don't even care about getting more work done. I just want to get the same amount of work done, but have more head space I can spend on things I enjoy

Everything I do with AI is in an effort to reach this north star

Use this prompt and watch the magic happen (feel free to just send this post to your agent)

items.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
items.content:
Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without <span>s everywhere, `<dialog>` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0])

Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent <div>+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.

200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]

I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.

We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)

People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.

Try it out:

    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

Longer write-up on the 1.0: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1

Stop saying AI doesn’t show judgment. 

Of course it shows judgment.

And actually, you already trust some of its judgment. 

When you ask it to find you an apartment and it goes on Zillow and not https://t.co/sUfKNrbqKz, that is judgment. 

When you ask it to make you a slideshow for a quick presentation to your boss on an extremely dense topic, it will only provide a few slides. That is judgment. 

When you’re replying to a question from a 7-year-old and their email is filled with emojis, and the AI writes like you but adds 1-2 emojis to better match the inbound email, that is judgment. 

Probabilistic models reasoning through infinite options toward a goal is “judgment”, though I’m not saying whether AI is literally judging - just that it is showing it. Researchers can weigh in on that nuance. 

Your personal judgment might be BETTER or WIDER, particularly if it’s in a field you are deeply familiar with, but let’s not pretend we don’t already partially rely on AI’s displayed judgment to get work done.

items.content:
I'm gonna try to keep this post to 57 seconds read, but these are the Claude tips you cannot afford to ignore:

1. Use the Claude desktop app (even after Cowork is gone)

Not 'Claude in browser'. The day you start using the app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files. You'd use Claude code more. Trust me, there is no coming back from there.

2. Always reach out for Opus 5.5 (not Fable 5.2)

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. Fable 5.2 is insanely good but burns your token in just 3-4 prompts. You won't be able to complete any task with Fable 5.2. 

3. Do not switch the Claude models mid-chat. 

It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal & end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

5. Turn your Claude Memory ON.

Claude team tested it with & without memory. With memory, Opus 5.5 scored 28% better. Just, click “+” in chat box → turn on 'Memory'.

6. But keep your memory short.

Claude had 105 facts about me before starting a session, but after one prompt, it came down to 26. To copy my exact prompt to clean memory, go to https://t.co/U9NLc2FuiR

7. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

8. Never argue with Claude. It is pointless.

You'll end up burning your tokens without finishing the task. Instead, click on “Edit” on your already sent prompt right before the bad answer. Change, edit, or fix. Click “Save”.

9. Delete your instructions box.

Remove “about me”, “how I write” file, list of rules. They all force Claude to limit its creativity. Aim to give one clear goal per prompt.

10. One Claude Project per client.

Inside the project, turn off “Use account memory”. Now what Claude knows about Client A doesn't get mixed up with Client B.

11. Ask for the spread.

When Claude gives you the most generic answer (that’s literally how it works). Push it to give you the weird, unlikely ones. Use this prompt:

“Give me 20 very different options. For each one, tell me how likely another AI would give it to me. The last two must be under 10%.”

12. Give Claude a finish line.

Define what 'done' means to you, by using these:

“Done means: a one-page doc my boss can forward without editing.”

13. Above tips barely scratched the surface of mastering Claude. To go even deeper, get the other 11 tips + prompts from the same guide: https://t.co/U9NLc2FuiR

The 7 Essential Layers of AI Agent Architecture

Building reliable AI agents requires more than LLMs and prompts.

Here are 7 layers every AI engineer should know.

01 - Models | Reasoning
Power decisions and tool selection.
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral

02 - Vector DB | Retrieval
Enable semantic search and RAG.
Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma, Redis

03 - Frameworks | Integration
Connect models, data, and tools.
LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack

04 - Orchestration | Execution
Manage workflows, state, and retries.
LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK

05 - APIs & Protocols | Connectivity
Enable tool access and agent communication.
MCP, A2A, REST, JSON-RPC

06 - Infrastructure | Scaling
Handle deployment and compute.
Docker, Kubernetes, AWS ECS, Modal

07 - Evaluation | Reliability
Monitor accuracy, failures, latency, and cost.
RAGAS, DeepEval, LangSmith, Langfuse

Key Takeaway
A working agent needs intelligence.

A production-ready agent needs architecture, security, and continuous evaluation.

🛠️🧭 "How We Solved Agent Building" got me digging.

If you are building AI Agents for real business workflows, you have probably struggled with:

agent handoffs, lost context, complex orchestration, failed tool calls, and agents that work in demos but struggle with real user questions.

I watched a talk on AI Engineer about how Vercel tried several agent architectures before a simple file system beat their multi-agent system.

So I pulled together their 6 stages and the open-source tools worth exploring at each one.

Here are 19 GitHub repos worth knowing for AI Agent building in 2026:

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟭: 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁

✸ Vercel AI SDK → unified model access  
✸ LiteLLM → multi-provider LLM gateway  
✸ Instructor → structured LLM outputs

→ Test whether the LLM can generate valid SQL.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟮: 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺

✸ LangGraph → stateful agent orchestration  
✸ CrewAI → role-based agent collaboration  
✸ Google ADK → multi-agent conversations  
✸ OpenAI Agents SDK → agents + handoffs

→ Specialized agents, but context gets lost in handoffs.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟯: 𝗢𝗻𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁

✸ PydanticAI → typed agents + dependencies  
✸ Deep Agents → planning + persistent context  
✸ Mastra → workflows + memory + tools

→ One agent can plan, execute, and recover from errors.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟰: 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁

✸ Claude Code → filesystem-based coding agent  
✸ just-bash → Bash + virtual filesystem  
✸ Vercel Sandbox → isolated code execution

→ File system + Bash roughly doubled the eval score.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟱: 𝗥𝗲𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀

✸ Anthropic Skills → reusable agent instructions  
✸ Skills CLI → discover + install skills  
✸ Vercel Agent Skills → domain-specific skills

→ Reuse proven workflows instead of starting from scratch.

》𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝟲: 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸

✸ Eve → filesystem-first agent framework  
✸ Workflow DevKit → durable execution  
✸ OpenTelemetry → tracing + observability
→ Turn files, tools, and skills into deployable agents.

And this is the architectural progression:

Big Prompt  
→ Multi-Agent System  
→ Stateful Agent  
→ File System + Bash  
→ Reusable Skills  
→ Production Runtime

Engineering Lead Bot・Jev を組み合わせると、かなり体験よく使えそうだし、Cursor Projects と合わせると、より効果的なので、私もすぐに試そうと思う！

3. 開発作業では pstack プラグインの Skill を最優先で検討してから使うよう指示する
4. 「どの Skill が必要か」はDecisions Model のJev に選ばせる

重要なのは Engineering Lead Bot で、この Bot が作業をCloud Agents に分けてくれるので、Outer Loop としてチケット役兼タスクの追跡をしてくれる

Cursor Agents でなく Cursor Projects を指定しても良いだろう

細分化したチケットをそのまま Coordinator Agent に渡せるし、Projects をチームで共有すれば、チームで使える Task Board が完成する

この Bot の原則は、CIの失敗・レビュー・止まっている作業を追跡し、PRマージ・作業の中止・ユーザーが引き取った時を完了とし、作業中は邪魔をしないように設計されている

持っているSkillは以下の5つだ

・engineering-lead-onboard：初回の設定。使うリポジトリ、作業管理ツール、レビューのルール、Bot として動くときの名義、ダイジェストを送る先を聞き取る。その後、平日のタスク追跡ルーティンをONにする

・engineering-lead-decompose：依頼を、それぞれ単独で出荷できる少数の Cloud Agent タスクか Project に分けて起動し、追跡

・engineering-lead-chase：追跡中のエージェントと PR を一通り見て回る。自分で解消できる詰まりは解消し、人の判断が必要なものだけ上げる

・engineering-lead-pr-attribution：Bot の名義で PR を作ったり更新したりするときの正しい手順を定義

・engineering-lead-digest：細かい更新を何通も送る代わりに、短い状況のまとめを書く

Google's team published a 9-page PDF on Harness Engineering. one formula replaced prompt engineering:

Agent = Model + Harness

the twist: same Claude Sonnet, same benchmark. change only the harness

the playbook, six steps:

step 1 -> add guides
AGENTS.md, rule files, constraint docs. every line is an old agent failure turned into a permanent fix

step 2 -> add sensors
linters, tests, validation scripts. the agent checks its own output before a human ever sees it

step 3 -> build the agentic loop
plan, execute, verify, fix. retries are capped, budgets are capped, and a stuck agent escalates

step 4 -> externalize memory
the model forgets every session. the harness keeps the state, the decisions and the artifacts

step 5 -> enforce permissions
which tools, how many writes, what needs approval. the harness owns safety

step 6 -> wire observability
every tool call, cost and retry gets tracked. a trip wire fires the moment behavior drifts

the result: your agent stops being a demo and becomes infrastructure

every failure turns into a permanent fix, so every next run starts smarter

that's the gap between an agent you demo and one a client pays you to leave running

one harness gives you a reliable loop. connect several and you get graph engineering, where one agent's failure becomes another agent's sensor

the PDF stops at the harness. the graph is the next layer
